# Book I, Proposition 20

*Two sides exceed the third*

> In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/20-idea.svg" alt="Lay any two sides of a triangle end to end (blue and yellow), and together they are longer than the third side (red)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Lay any two sides of a triangle end to end (blue and yellow), and together they are longer than the third side (red).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/20.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.20, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let ABC be a triangle;

I say that in the triangle ABC two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one, namely

BA, AC greater than BC,

AB, BC greater than AC,

BC, CA greater than AB.

For let BA be drawn through to the point D,

let DA be made equal to CA, and let DC be joined.

Then, since DA is equal to AC,

the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]

therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]

And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,

and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]

therefore DB is greater than BC.

But DA is equal to AC;

therefore BA, AC are greater than BC.

Similarly we can prove that AB, BC are also greater than CA, and BC, CA than AB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop20.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop20.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one. -/
theorem Prop20 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) :
    ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖ := by
  -- For let ABC be a triangle;
  -- I say that in the triangle ABC two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the
  -- remaining one, namely
  -- BA, AC greater than BC,
  -- AB, BC greater than AC,
  -- BC, CA greater than AB.
  /- Euclid proves the first, and says "similarly" for the other two. So we give his
     argument for every triangle, in his letters, and use it three times below. -/
  have greater : ∀ {A B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
    intro A B C hABC
    have hB_A : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    obtain ⟨BA, hB_BA, hA_BA⟩ := Postulate1 B A hB_A
    have hC_BA : ¬ OnLine C BA := hABC.bac.off_line hB_BA hA_BA
    -- For let BA be drawn through to the point D,
    /- Drawn through beyond A to a point X, far enough for I.3 to cut AD off from AX:
       `produce_longer` in Book Zero. -/
    obtain ⟨X, hBAX, hAC_AX⟩ := produce_longer hB_A hA_C
    -- let DA be made equal to CA, and let DC be joined.
    /- Heath gives no bracket here, but "let DA be made equal" is I.3's work, as in
       I.11 and I.16: cut off AD from AX. Then D lies between A and X, and so A lies
       between B and D (`between_cut`): BA drawn through reaches D. -/
    obtain ⟨D, hADX, hAD_CA⟩ := Prop3 (A := A) (B := X) hA_C.symm
      (by rw [len_symm C A]; exact hAC_AX)
    have hBAD : Between B A D := between_cut hBAX hADX
    have hD_BA : OnLine D BA := on_line_of_between hBAD hB_BA hA_BA
    have hA_D : A ≠ D := ne_of_between hADX
    have hD_C : D ≠ C := fun e => hC_BA (e ▸ hD_BA)
    obtain ⟨DC, hD_DC, hC_DC⟩ := Postulate1 D C hD_C
    -- Then, since DA is equal to AC,
    have hDA_AC : ‖D A‖ = ‖A C‖ := by rw [len_symm D A, hAD_CA, len_symm C A]
    -- the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]
    /- I.5 for the triangle ADC, whose sides AD, AC are equal. Its statement also
       speaks of the equal sides produced, so Lean produces them (Post. 2,
       `Prop5.base`), though only the angles at the base are wanted here. -/
    have hADC : Triangle A D C := Triangle.of_line hA_BA hD_BA hA_D hC_BA
    have hADC_ACD : ∠ A D C = ∠ A C D :=
      Prop5.base hADC (by rw [← len_symm D A]; exact hDA_AC)
    -- therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]
    /- Greater than the angle ACD, which is equal to it: CA falls within the angle
       BCD, since A lies between B and D, so that the angle BCD is made up of the
       angles BCA and ACD (`angle_add_of_between`); the angle BCA, an angle of the
       triangle ABC, is something (`Triangle.angle_pos`); and the whole is greater
       than the part. -/
    have hBDC : Triangle B D C :=
      Triangle.of_line hB_BA hD_BA (ne_of_between_ends hBAD) hC_BA
    have hADC_BCD : ∠ A D C < ∠ B C D := by
      rw [hADC_ACD, angle_add_of_between hBDC hBAD, add_comm]
      exact CommonNotion5 hABC.bca.angle_pos
    -- And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,
    /- The angle BDC is the angle ADC, since A lies on the ray from D through B
       (`angle_onRay_left`). -/
    have hDCB : Triangle D C B := hBDC.bca
    have hBDC_BCD : ∠ B D C < ∠ B C D := by
      rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hBAD)) hD_C.symm]
      exact hADC_BCD
    -- and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]
    /- I.19 for the triangle BCD, named from B: the angle at C is greater than the
       angle at D, so the side BD, opposite C, is greater than the side BC, opposite
       D. -/
    have hBC_BD : ‖B C‖ < ‖B D‖ :=
      Prop19 hDCB.cba (by rw [angle_symm hD_C.symm (ne_of_between_ends hBAD)]; exact hBDC_BCD)
    -- therefore DB is greater than BC.
    have hBC_DB : ‖B C‖ < ‖D B‖ := by rw [len_symm D B]; exact hBC_BD
    -- But DA is equal to AC;
    /- And DB is BA and AD together, since A lies between B and D (System E,
       Diagram-segment 1); so DB is BA and AC together. -/
    have hDB : ‖D B‖ = ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
      rw [← hDA_AC, len_symm D A, len_add_of_between hBAD, len_symm D B]
    -- therefore BA, AC are greater than BC.
    rw [← hDB]
    exact hBC_DB
  /- Euclid's argument, in his own figure: BA, AC are greater than BC. -/
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := greater hABC
  -- Similarly we can prove that AB, BC are also greater than CA, and BC, CA than AB.
  /- The same argument for the triangle BAC, with AB drawn through beyond B, and for
     the triangle CBA, with BC drawn through beyond C. -/
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ := greater hABC.bac
  have hAB : ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖ := by
    rw [len_symm A B]
    exact greater hABC.cba
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hBC, hAC, hAB⟩
  -- Q. E. D.
```

If `C` and `D` are on the same side of `L`, and `B` and `D` are not on the same side of `M`, then `B` and `C` are on the same side of `N`: `C` lies within the angle `BAD`. (Triple incidence 2)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle `ABC` can be applied to the straight line `L` with `A` on `D`, `B` on the ray from `D` through `G`, and `C` on the side of `L` where `H` is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L22): Adding is associative. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L25): Adding is commutative. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L44): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L28): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L31): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L34): "Less than" is transitive. (System E §3.5)

## Mishnah

**Evident even to an ass.** "It was the habit of the Epicureans, says Proclus (p. 323), to ridicule this theorem as being evident even to an ass and requiring no proof": put fodder at one corner of a triangle and the ass at another, and he goes along the one side between them, not the other two. Savile thought the Epicureans fit to eat hay with the ass. "Proclus replies truly that a mere perception of the truth of the theorem is a different thing from a scientific proof of it and a knowledge of the reason why it is true. Moreover, as Simson says, the number of axioms should not be increased without necessity" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 287). Lean takes Simson's side: no tacit rule states the theorem, so I.20 is proved, as Euclid proves it, from I.5 and I.19.

**Room to cut off AD.** Euclid's "let DA be made equal to CA" has no bracket, but it is I.3's work, as in I.11 and I.16, and I.3 cuts off only from a greater straight line. Book Zero's `produce_longer` makes room: a circle about A through C (Post. 3) is cut by BA produced beyond the centre (System E, Intersections 5), and BA produced a little further (Post. 2) is greater than AC (Def. 15). I.3 cuts AD off it, and `between_cut` puts A between B and D.

**What Lean made us say.** Euclid's "therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC" carries the bracket [C.N. 5]: greater, that is, than ACD, which I.5 has just made equal to it. So CA must fall within the angle BCD, and it does, because A lies between B and D (`angle_add_of_between`, with `Triangle.angle_pos` for the part BCA). Euclid then writes BDC for ADC, one angle since A lies on the ray from D through B (`angle_onRay_left`); DCB is a triangle, C being off BD (`Triangle.of_line`); and DB is BA and AD together (System E, Diagram-segment 1).

**"Similarly."** Euclid proves that BA, AC are greater than BC and leaves the other two pairs to the reader. The Lean gives his argument once, for every triangle, and uses it three times, naming the triangle from each corner in turn (`Triangle.bac`, `Triangle.cba`).

**The modern way.** For vectors u and v, |u + v|² = |u|² + 2u·v + |v|², and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality u·v ≤ |u||v| makes this at most (|u| + |v|)², with equality only when u and v point the same way. In the complex plane it reads |z + w| ≤ |z| + |w|, and what Euclid proves, the theory of metric spaces takes as part of the definition of distance: the triangle inequality.
